title: Sikh soldiers in the World Wars
word: Sikh soldiers in the World Wars
hook: tens of thousands of Sikhs served and many died in both world wars, far from Punjab

segments.voice: Yesterday, the SGPC, and your line, peaceful protest worked. Did you speak up once, calmly? Today is day three hundred on this path. Thank you for walking it. And today, Sikhs who walked a very long way from home. Day three hundred.

Autumn, 1914. A young farmer from a village in Punjab steps off a ship in France. He has never seen the sea before this journey. He has never felt cold like this. Within days he's in a muddy trench in Flanders, in a war between European empires he'd barely heard of a year ago, wearing his turban under the gray sky. In his pocket, maybe, a small book of prayers. At home, his mother is waiting for a letter. Today: Sikh soldiers in the World Wars.
screen: `AUTUMN, 1914, FRANCE.` → `A PUNJABI FARMER IN A TRENCH.` → `HIS MOTHER WAITING FOR A LETTER.`

segments.voice: When the First World War began, India was ruled by Britain, and the Indian Army was sent to fight. Sikhs made up a large part of it, far more than their share of India's population. They were among the first Indian troops to reach the Western Front in 1914, holding lines at Ypres and fighting at Neuve Chapelle. Others served at Gallipoli, in Mesopotamia, in East Africa. Tens of thousands of Sikhs served, and many never came home. Many of their letters home survive, because the army censors copied out and translated extracts. They talk about the cold, the guns, friends lost, and again and again about God, and about the village. Some ask that the family keep praying at the gurdwara. Twenty-five years later it happened again. In the Second World War Sikh soldiers fought in North Africa, in Italy, in Malaya, and in the jungles of Burma, where a Sikh soldier named Nand Singh won the Victoria Cross, Britain's highest award for bravery. Why did they go? Historians give many answers. Many were from farming families, and soldiering was steady pay and honored work. Many had a strong military tradition, and a sense of duty. Most were volunteers, though not all went freely. And it's a hard truth that they fought for an empire that did not let their own people rule themselves. For a long time, their part was mostly left out of the story of the wars. That's changing. Today there are memorials to Sikh soldiers in France, in Britain, and in Punjab. They served and died far from Punjab, and they're remembered.
screen: `1914: FROM PUNJAB TO FLANDERS.` · `LETTERS HOME, ABOUT GOD AND THE VILLAGE.` · `1939–45: AFRICA, ITALY, BURMA.` · `LONG LEFT OUT, NOW REMEMBERED.` · then, large: `FAR FROM PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who has served: in the military, as a nurse, a firefighter, a caregiver, someone who went far from home to do a hard job for others. Maybe someone in your own family history. Picture them, and picture the people waiting for their letters. Silently, say thank you to them. If they're living and you can, plan to say it out loud. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember their soldiers of both world wars at memorials in France, Britain and Punjab and at Remembrance Day services, where Sikh groups often lay wreaths and say Ardas for the fallen.

what a scholar hears: Sikhs formed a disproportionate share of the Indian Army in 1914–18; the censored letters of Indian soldiers survive in the British Library; Naik Nand Singh won the VC in the Arakan, Burma, in 1944.
